title: Episode 1 (lines 249–694)

teacherSummary.text: Oedipus defends himself: he acted in self-defence and without knowledge. Ismene brings news that his sons are fighting over Thebes and that an oracle says whoever holds Oedipus' grave will prosper, so Creon is coming for him. Oedipus curses his sons, purifies the grove through Ismene, and answers the elders' questions about the incest and the killing. Theseus arrives, recalls that he too was an exile, and grants Oedipus protection.

He even calls it “That was my bane” (line 533). The diction lets the elders hear the worst name for the marriage without granting that he chose it.
The outcast becomes a treasure a city may want to keep and protect

The sons, as Oedipus tells it, heard the oracle and still chose power: they “sacrificed their sire / For lust of power and sceptred sovereignty” (lines 448–449), and they “spoke no word” when “one little word from them / Was all I needed” (lines 442–443). Theseus, who has never owed him that kinship, answers a stranger out of known hardship: “no alien in adversity / Shall seek in vain my succour, nor shalt thou” (lines 586–587). The contrast is between blood that failed and a host who knows what exile is.

Oedipus says the benefit of the body he offers will come “When I am dead and thou hast buried me” (line 603): the worth is postponed until the grave is in Theseus's keeping. Theseus answers not with curiosity about the mystery but with a present personal bond: “Fear not for me; I shall not play thee false” (line 673). The close therefore keeps the future grave in view while making the living man already a protected guest of Athens.

anchorPassages.text:
The toil and trouble, father, that I bore
To find thy lodging-place and how thou faredst,
I spare thee; surely ’twere a double pain
To suffer, first in act and then in telling;
’Tis the misfortune of thine ill-starred sons
I come to tell thee. At the first they willed
To leave the throne to Creon, minded well
Thus to remove the inveterate curse of old,
A canker that infected all thy race.
But now some god and an infatuate soul
Have stirred betwixt them a mad rivalry
To grasp at sovereignty and kingly power.
Today the hot-brained youth, the younger born,
Is keeping Polyneices from the throne,
His elder, and has thrust him from the land.
The banished brother (so all Thebes reports)
Fled to the vale of Argos, and by help
Of new alliance there and friends in arms,
Swears he will stablish Argos straight as lord
Of the Cadmeian land, or, if he fail,
Exalt the victor to the stars of heaven.
This is no empty tale, but deadly truth,
My father; and how long thy agony,
Ere the gods pity thee, I cannot tell.

Thy country (so it runs) shall yearn in time
To have thee for their weal alive or dead.
And who could gain by such a one as I?
On thee, ’tis said, their sovereignty depends.
So, when I cease to be, my worth begins.
The gods, who once abased, uplift thee now.
Poor help to raise an old man fallen in youth.
Howe’er that be, ’tis for this cause alone
That Creon comes to thee—and comes anon.
With what intent, my daughter? Tell me plainly.
To plant thee near the Theban land, and so
Keep thee within their grasp, yet not allow
Thy foot to pass beyond their boundaries.
What gain they, if I lie outside?

Then may the gods ne’er quench their fatal feud,
And mine be the arbitrament of the fight,
For which they now are arming, spear to spear;
That neither he who holds the scepter now
May keep his throne, nor he who fled the realm
Return again. They never raised a hand,
When I their sire was thrust from hearth and home;
When I was banned and banished, what recked they?
Say you ’twas done at my desire, a grace
Which the State, yielding to my wish, allowed?
Not so; for, mark you, on that very day
When in the tempest of my soul I craved
Death, even death by stoning, none appeared
To further that wild longing, but anon,
When time had numbed my anguish and I felt
My wrath had all outrun those errors past,
Then, then it was the city went about
By force to oust me, respited for years;
And they my sons, who should as sons have helped,
Did nothing: and, one little word from them
Was all I needed, and they spoke no word,
But let me wander on forevermore,

Oft had I heard of thee in times gone by—
The bloody mutilation of thine eyes—
And therefore know thee, son of Laius.
All that I lately gathered on the way
Made my conjecture doubly sure; and now
Thy garb and that marred visage prove to me
That thou art he. So pitying thine estate,
Most ill-starred Oedipus, I fain would know
What is the suit ye urge on me and Athens,
Thou and the helpless maiden at thy side.
Declare it; dire indeed must be the tale
Whereat I should recoil. I too was reared,
Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands
Wrestled with many perils, no man more.
Wherefore no alien in adversity
Shall seek in vain my succour, nor shalt thou;
I know myself a mortal, and my share
In what the morrow brings no more than thine.

I come to offer thee this woe-worn frame,
A gift not fair to look on; yet its worth
More precious far than any outward show.
What profit dost thou proffer to have brought?
Hereafter thou shalt learn, not yet, methinks.
When may we hope to reap the benefit?
When I am dead and thou hast buried me.
Thou cravest life’s last service; all before—
Is it forgotten or of no account?
Yea, the last boon is warrant for the rest.
The grace thou cravest then is small indeed.
Nay, weigh it well; the issue is not slight.

anchorPassages.note: Friendship between cities decays; the hero's grave will decide the quarrel.
anchorPassages.text:
Dear son of Aegeus, to the gods alone
Is given immunity from eld and death;
But nothing else escapes all-ruinous time.
Earth’s might decays, the might of men decays,
Honour grows cold, dishonour flourishes,
There is no constancy ’twixt friend and friend,
Or city and city; be it soon or late,
Sweet turns to bitter, hate once more to love.
If now ’tis sunshine betwixt Thebes and thee
And not a cloud, Time in his endless course
Gives birth to endless days and nights, wherein
The merest nothing shall suffice to cut
With serried spears your bonds of amity.
Then shall my slumbering and buried corse
In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up,
If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true.
No more: ’tis ill to tear aside the veil
Of mysteries; let me cease as I began:
Enough if thou wilt keep thy plighted troth,
Then shalt thou ne’er complain that Oedipus
Proved an unprofitable and thankless guest,
Except the gods themselves shall play me false.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Yet am I then / A villain born because in self-defence, / Stricken, I struck the striker back again” slowly and put it in my own words: Oedipus asks whether he is a villain just because, when he was struck, he struck back in self-defense. The strongest word is “Stricken”: “Stricken” comes first, so the listener hears the blow he received before the blow he gave. Then, effect. items.text: What does "So, when I cease to be, my worth begins" mean?
items.lookFor: His value to a city will begin with his death: Ismene’s report that his country will want him “alive or dead” turns the outcast into something worth possessing.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus is answering Ismene’s report that his country “shall yearn in time / To have thee for their weal alive or dead” (lines 389–390). His dry reply, “So, when I cease to be, my worth begins” (line 393), means that the man everyone rejected while he lived becomes valuable at the moment of death, because whoever holds his body holds its power. The line is bitter as well as hopeful.

items.text: What does “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)” suggest about Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: An inference that joins the two halves of the scene: Thebes wants Oedipus as a possession to control, while Theseus receives him as a person with rights, so possession is set against hospitality.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Thebes wants him only as an asset. Ismene says they mean “To plant thee near the Theban land, and so / Keep thee within their grasp” (lines 399–400). Theseus offers the opposite and will “grant him the full rights of citizen” (line 661). The scene suggests that the same man can be treated as property or as a guest with rights, and that this difference will decide where he ends his life.

items.text: Find one example of characterization in “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)”. What does it reveal about Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: A trait shown in action and what it reveals beyond a label, such as Theseus meeting the same reputation the elders feared with pity, or Oedipus praising his daughters’ care while condemning his sons.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Theseus has heard the same story that frightened the elders (“Oft had I heard of thee in times gone by,” line 572), but it moves him to pity, not fear: “So pitying thine estate” (line 578), he asks what Oedipus wants. The characterization shows that the difference between the elders and their king is not what they know about Oedipus but how they respond to it.

items.text: How does the theme in “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)” shape what we understand about Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome?
items.lookFor: How the theme of guilt and intent, argued in Oedipus’s defence (“all unwitting,” “without intent”), changes how we read the welcome: Theseus receives a man who has made a case that suffering and guilt differ.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The scene keeps returning to guilt and intent. Oedipus says “all unwitting whither I went, I went” (line 265) and “I slew without intent, / A wretch, but innocent / In the law’s eye” (lines 567–569). Because this case is argued before Theseus enters, his welcome reads as more than kindness: he receives a man who has argued that a terrible deed done without knowledge does not make him a villain.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “O what avails renown…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from Oedipus’s opening speech (lines 249–283) with their connotations, such as “renown,” “vanity,” “dislodged” or “scutcheon,” showing how he turns Athens’ reputation into an obligation.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The word “renown” (line 249) and the phrase “Athens’ fair scutcheon” (line 275) both point to reputation: Athens is famous for sheltering strangers, and its coat of arms could be stained. By choosing honour words instead of pleas for pity, Oedipus makes driving him out a threat to the city’s good name, which is harder for the elders to ignore.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn is Ismene’s news (the feud, the oracles, Creon coming), which changes Oedipus from a man asking to stay into a man with something to give and withhold. The effect: he refuses Thebes and offers himself to Athens.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn is Ismene’s report that the oracles now make Oedipus valuable and that “Creon comes to thee—and comes anon” (line 397). It changes his stance. He refuses Thebes (“Then never shall they be my masters, never!”, line 410) and offers himself to his hosts as “A great deliverer, for my foemen bane” (line 459). The likely effect is a struggle over him, with Thebes trying to reclaim what Athens now protects.

items.text: How does “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)” build on “Parodos (lines 115–248)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A cause-and-effect link: the elders’ refusal at the end of the Parodos leaves Oedipus to answer in words, and his defence persuades them to leave the decision to their king.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The Parodos ends with the elders refusing to change their ruling (lines 247–248). Episode 1 opens with his answer: “Have I so found it? I whom ye dislodged / First from my seat of rock and now would drive / Forth from your land” (lines 254–256). The argument works well enough that they agree to “leave the issue with the ruling powers” (line 286), which is why the king comes.

items.text: In “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: A motive beneath a claim: Oedipus calls his request small (burial), but his aim is to choose where his power will rest and to defeat those who cast him out.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus says the benefit he brings comes only “When I am dead and thou hast buried me” (line 603), and Theseus calls the favour “small indeed” (line 607). His real motive shows a few lines later: “Here shall I vanquish those who cast me forth” (line 670). He wants his last resting place to be a judgment on Thebes and on his sons, not only a kindness to himself.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (When has your own experience helped you understand someone else?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer that uses Theseus’s own exile as the example of experience creating understanding, and notes how it changes his response compared with the elders’.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: My first answer was about understanding a friend after the same loss. Episode 1 gives a sharper example. Theseus understands Oedipus because “I too was reared, / Like thee, in exile” (lines 583–584), and so “no alien in adversity / Shall seek in vain my succour” (lines 586–587). The elders judged by the name; Theseus judges by shared experience, and that changes the outcome.

items.text: Where does conflict appear in “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)”, and how does it connect Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome to the larger concern with curse and mercy?
items.lookFor: Conflict located in the scene (Oedipus against his absent sons, or Thebes against Athens over him) and tied to curse and mercy: the father curses sons who showed him none, while a stranger shows mercy.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The sharpest conflict is between Oedipus and his absent sons. Because “one little word from them / Was all I needed, and they spoke no word” (lines 442–443), he prays, “may the gods ne’er quench their fatal feud” (line 423). That is the curse half; the mercy half comes from a stranger, as Theseus asks, “Who could reject / The proffered amity of such a friend?” (lines 654–655). The scene sets a father’s curse on his kin against a stranger’s mercy.

items.text: Is Oedipus innocent? Evaluate his argument in lines 261–263 against the play's other evidence.
items.lookFor: An evaluation of the self-defence argument (lines 261–263) against other evidence in the play, his “all unwitting” and “innocent / In the law’s eye” and what still troubles it (he did kill; he calls his sufferings vile), with a position and a counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: innocent of intent, not of the deed. His claim that he struck “in self-defence, / Stricken” (lines 262–263) is backed by “I slew who else would me have slain” (line 566) and by his acting “all unwitting” (line 265). Counter-line: he admits, “Yes, a murderer” (line 562), and that he “suffered ills most vile” (line 527). The play lets him be innocent in law and still marked by what he did.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The outcast becomes a treasure once Athens receives him, reversing the expulsion from Thebes. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines: support from “So, when I cease to be, my worth begins” and Theseus’s grant of citizenship, with a qualification that the treasure is also a threat to his enemies.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, with a qualification. Oedipus names the reversal himself, “So, when I cease to be, my worth begins” (line 393), and Theseus receives him with “the full rights of citizen” (line 661), the opposite of being cast out. But the treasure is not harmless: Oedipus says that if Thebes turns on Athens, his buried body will “drink their warm life-blood up” (line 643). He is a gift to his hosts and a threat to his enemies at once.

items.text: Which character in “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)” acts most wisely in the matter of Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to two characters, for example judging only on full knowledge: Theseus waits to hear everything, while Oedipus curses his sons on a report. Give a line for each.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of judging only on full knowledge, Theseus acts most wisely: “Say on, I wait full knowledge ere I judge” (line 616). By the same standard Oedipus acts least wisely when he curses his sons, praying that “neither he who holds the scepter now / May keep his throne” (lines 426–427), on the strength of Ismene’s report. A student could defend Oedipus by another standard, justice to a neglected father, since his sons “spoke no word” for him (line 443).

items.text: You are directing “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as Ismene’s entrance seen through Antigone’s uncertainty or Theseus physically closing the distance at his welcome, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) Let Ismene be heard before she is seen. Antigone peers offstage, asking “She or a stranger? Do I wake or dream?” (line 308), so the audience shares the family’s suspense about whether this is help or danger. (2) When Theseus says “I too was reared, / Like thee, in exile” (lines 583–584), have him walk to the seated Oedipus and kneel to his level, the first character to come close instead of standing off. The welcome becomes physical, not only spoken.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 249–694: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: What must be poured, and with what, to atone to the goddesses? (Water and honey, “add no wine,” line 482, from bowls crowned with wool, then olive sprays, lines 468–485.) Why/how: Why does Theseus pity Oedipus instead of fearing him? (He was himself an exile, lines 583–585.) Should/what if: Should Oedipus have refused the elders’ questions about his past? (Answers weigh his request, “as guest I claim / This grace” (lines 518–519), against the elders’ wish to know whom they shelter.)

items.text: Connect “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)”, with its focus on Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome, to law against force: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about law against force, the question’s theme. Oedipus appeals to law and Theseus answers the threat from Thebes with a public pledge, but force is only threatened. A strong answer names what must come next.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is stronger than in the Parodos but still promised, not tested. Oedipus claims to stand “innocent / In the law’s eye” (lines 568–569), and Theseus answers the threat from Thebes with a pledge, “I know that none / Shall hale thee hence in my despite” (lines 685–686). No one has yet used force. To strengthen the link, Sophocles needs to show force actually tried against Athens’ word, and the land’s law answering it.

items.text: Is the characterization in “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)” effective in presenting Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment of the characterization against a criterion (complex or one-note?), for example Oedipus’s tenderness and bitterness in one scene, and whether Theseus is too ideal.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because Oedipus is shown with mixed qualities in one scene. He praises Antigone’s “tender ministry” (line 351) and soon after wishes his sons an unending “fatal feud” (line 423). Counter-line: Theseus may seem too ideal, generous at every turn (“Thy choice is mine,” line 665). A reviewer could call him heavy-handed, a model king rather than a person. A strong answer decides whether that idealism serves the play’s argument about hospitality.

items.text: Compare how “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)” treats Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (a story of a refugee or exile welcomed by a host) and one thing Episode 1 sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: News stories about refugees often treat the host’s generosity as the whole story. Episode 1 adds a harder truth: the guest brings old family wars with him. Theseus welcomes Oedipus, but Oedipus warns that between friends and cities “Sweet turns to bitter, hate once more to love” (line 636). The play sees that hospitality may draw the host into the guest’s conflicts, which the simpler story leaves out.

items.text: Predict what “Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues at the end of the episode, Theseus placing Oedipus in the elders’ charge and calling the place god-chosen, about what the elders will now sing, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: Theseus says, “I place him in your charge” (line 663), so the elders now have a duty to the man they tried to expel. Clue 2: he tells Oedipus, “Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here” (line 693), presenting the place as chosen by a god. A reasonable prediction is that the elders will praise their land and why it is fit to receive him. After reading, students check whether the ode praises Colonus, Athens or Oedipus.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Episode 1 (lines 249–694)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about Ismene's news; Theseus' welcome?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: a rejected man learns he has become valuable to the people who rejected him, while a host offers him rights. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: A disgraced scientist living abroad learns that his home government now wants him back, not to welcome him but to control his work, while a foreign mayor who was once a refugee offers him citizenship. Two things must stay: the home country’s wish to keep him “within their grasp” (line 400) without letting him in, and the host’s fellow-feeling born of his own exile (lines 583–584).
